opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a sudden decision. It happened gradually, and it came from a mix of curiosity and a feeling about where the field's energy was going.

I really loved formal methods. Working on SMT solvers and verification taught me to think rigorously: to ask what a system is actually guaranteed to do, not just what it seems to do on a few examples. That mindset has stayed with me. But during my PhD I started to feel that progress in that area was steady and incremental, while something very different was happening in AI. Large language models were suddenly doing things that, a few years earlier, most of us would have said were far away.

What really pulled me in was that these models were incredibly powerful but also incredibly expensive and hard to run. Very few people could actually serve them or experiment with them. That struck me as a systems problem, and it was exactly the kind of problem I knew how to think about. How do you squeeze a huge model onto limited hardware? How do you schedule requests, manage memory, and reuse computation so that inference becomes cheap enough for everyone? Those questions felt urgent, and you could see the impact almost immediately. You build something, you open-source it, and within weeks thousands of people are using it.

That fast feedback loop was very exciting compared with the longer time horizons in verification. And I didn't see it as abandoning my background. In some ways it's a continuation. The habit of reasoning carefully about correctness and structure helps a lot when you design runtimes and programming interfaces for LLMs. I also think the two worlds will come back together. As AI systems get more capable, questions about reliability, guarantees, and verification will matter even more.

So the short answer is that I followed the problems I found most alive at the time, and AI systems was where I felt I could have the biggest impact.

r002.rationale: It contrasts verification’s longer time horizons with AI’s faster feedback and impact, but does not attribute the move to dissatisfaction with verification’s limited real-world impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a clean break. I started my PhD at Stanford working on program verification, and I genuinely loved it. There's something beautiful about being able to prove a piece of code is correct instead of just hoping your tests cover enough. But as I went deeper, I kept running into the same wall: the systems I could verify were small, and the systems people actually cared about were huge and messy. The gap between what formal methods could handle and what the real world needed felt like it was growing, not shrinking.

Around the same time, large language models started to get genuinely good. And what struck me was that they were taking the opposite approach. No guarantees, no proofs, but they could handle messy, real-world scale problems that formal tools couldn't touch. At first that bothered me, because it felt like giving up on rigor. But then I realized the interesting problems were in the middle. How do you make these models efficient enough to deploy? How do you give them structure, like constrained decoding, so the output is actually well-formed? That's where my background turned out to be useful.

So I ended up working on LLM serving systems, things like SGLang, and that's where it clicked for me. It's still systems work. You still care about correctness and efficiency. You're just applying those instincts to a technology that's moving incredibly fast and that millions of people are actually using. For me, that was a trade worth making. I'd rather have a huge impact with imperfect tools than a perfect proof about something few people use.

r001.rationale: The response says verification applied to small systems while real-world systems were huge and messy, but it does not state that verification’s cost was disproportionate to its reach.

r002.rationale: The response connects the move toward AI to the limited real-world scale of systems formal methods could handle and says the real-world gap was growing.

r003.rationale: The response says nothing about Ying Sheng’s publication record or gaps in her research trajectory.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was a shift in the kinds of problems I wanted to work on. Formal methods and program verification ask a very precise question: given a specification, can we prove that a program behaves correctly? That’s a powerful way of thinking, but it also depends on being able to specify what we want.

What drew me toward AI was the possibility of tackling problems where that specification is difficult to write down—where we can provide examples or feedback, but not a complete set of rules. I became more interested in how systems could learn those behaviors.

I still see a connection between the two fields. Building a capable system raises questions about how to understand it, evaluate it, and trust its behavior. The habits of thinking carefully about assumptions and correctness remain valuable, even when a formal proof isn’t available.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of specifying desired behavior, but does not say verification was costly relative to how little it could verify.

r002.rationale: The response describes interest in AI problems that are hard to specify, but does not attribute the move to dissatisfaction with program verification’s limited real-world impact.

r003.rationale: The response says nothing about Ying Sheng’s publication record or gaps in her research trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was less about moving away from formal methods and more about wanting to tackle a different part of the problem. In program verification, you start with a specification and ask whether a program satisfies it. That’s a powerful approach, but specifying exactly what you want can itself be very difficult.

What attracted me to AI was the possibility of learning from examples and handling tasks where we don’t have a complete, precise specification. It opens up a much broader set of problems.

And I see a connection between the two. As AI becomes more capable, questions about correctness and reliability become more important. So the way of thinking I learned from formal methods still feels very relevant.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI offers a broader range of problems, but does not attribute the move to dissatisfaction with program verification’s limited real-world impact.
